title: Davenant: concurrent conditions, not meritorious causes
source_text: LIV. Praesertim vero hac in parte Reformatorum sententiam accurate exponit & illustrat Davenantius, de Justitia actuali, capite 31. ubi haec est quinta illius conclusio: Bona quaedam opera sunt necessaria ad justificationem, ut conditiones concurrentes, vel praecursoriae, licet non sint necessaria, ut causae efficientes, aut meritoriae. Cui statim subjungit, In hisce bonis operibus numero illa interna, quae apud Deum magni momenti sunt, quamvis in hominum oculos non incurrant, ut dolere de peccato, detestari pecca-tum, humiliter se Deo subjicere, ad Dei misericordiam confugere, in Christo Media-tore spem figere, novae vitae propositum inire, aliaque consimilia. Divina enim mise-ricordia non justificat stipites, hoc est, nihil agentes; neque equos & mulos, hoc est, recalcitrantes, & libidinibus suis obstinate adhaerescentes; sed homines, eosdemque com-punctos & contritos, ac Verbi Spiritusque divini ductum sequentes. Quemadmodum igitur ad sanitatem aegrotantis requiritur, ut morbum sentiat, sanitatem appetat, me-dicum adeat, morbum detegat, pharmacum recipiat; neque tamen ulla harum actionum, aut illis omnibus conjunctim sumptis, tanquam causis proprie meritoriis, aut proprie ef-ficientibus, consequitur valetudinem, sed sola opera medici, & virtute pharmaci: sic ad justificationem obtinendam requiruntur quidem actus, aut praecedentes aut concurren-tes; non tamen illorum efficacia, aut merito justificationem adipiscimur, sed gratia Dei miserantis & opitulantis nobis, atque virtute divini illius pharmaci, sanguinis Christi scilicet, quo animae leprosae & morbidae abluuntur & curantur.
pass_a_gloss: But especially in this part Davenant accurately expounds and illustrates the Reformers' mind, On Actual Righteousness, chapter 31, where this is his fifth conclusion: Certain good works are necessary to justification as concurrent or precursor conditions, although they are not necessary as efficient or meritorious causes. To which he at once adds: In these good works I number those internal ones which are of great moment with God, although they do not strike men's eyes—such as to grieve for sin, to detest sin, humbly to subject oneself to God, to flee to God's mercy, to fix hope in Christ the Mediator, to enter upon a purpose of new life, and other like things. For divine mercy does not justify logs—that is, those who do nothing; nor horses and mules—that is, those who kick back and obstinately cling to their lusts; but men, and the same pricked and contrite, and following the leading of the divine Word and Spirit. As therefore for the health of a sick man it is required that he feel the disease, desire health, go to the physician, uncover the disease, receive the medicine; and yet by none of these actions, or by all of them taken together as properly meritorious or properly efficient causes, does he obtain health, but only by the work of the physician and by the virtue of the medicine: so for obtaining justification certain acts, either preceding or concurrent, are indeed required; yet we do not obtain justification by their efficacy or merit, but by the grace of God pitying and helping us, and by the virtue of that divine medicine, namely the blood of Christ, by which leprous and diseased souls are washed and cured.
pass_b_english: Davenant: some good works are necessary as concurrent/precursory conditions, not as efficient or meritorious causes.
Mercy does not justify logs or stubborn mules but contrite followers of Word and Spirit—like a patient cooperating yet healed by the physician's remedy (Christ's blood).
